tagline: Under Michigan no-fault, a motorcycle is not a motor vehicle. That one definition decides who pays a rider’s medical bills after a crash in the Orchard Lake roundabout, on Grand River, or at the I-696 interchange, and whether there is a no-fault claim at all.

c.v: A motorcycle crash in Farmington Hills is governed by a rule many riders learn only after they are hurt: under Michigan no-fault, a motorcycle is not a “motor vehicle.” That definition decides who pays your medical bills, how much they pay, whether you have a no-fault claim at all, and how the insurer will argue the helmet question. Farmington Hills adds its own risks: the multilane roundabout at Orchard Lake Road and 14 Mile, which recorded 109 crashes in 2024, sixth among all Michigan intersections; drivers turning left across Grand River, Twelve Mile, Middlebelt, and the mile roads; the merges where I-696, I-96, I-275, and M-5 meet; and three road agencies, each with its own notice clock when the road itself caused the crash.

sections.heading: Where Farmington Hills motorcycle crashes happen

c.v: The Orchard Lake roundabout at 14 Mile.

A roundabout lowers speeds and turns most car crashes into sideswipes and rear-ends, which is why this one recorded 109 crashes but only 5 injuries in 2024. For a rider, a sideswipe is not minor. The roundabout crashes that injure riders are a driver entering without yielding to traffic already circulating, a driver in the inner lane exiting across the outer lane where the motorcycle is, and a driver changing lanes inside the circle. A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane (MCL 257.660(2)), and a driver who crowds a rider out of it is at fault.
Orchard Lake between 12 Mile and 14 Mile.

A driver pulling out of a retail or office driveway into the near lane, looking for a gap among cars, often misses a motorcycle in that gap. At the 12 Mile signal, which recorded 65 crashes and 16 injuries in 2024, red-light and turning crashes add to it.
The left turn on Grand River, Twelve Mile, Middlebelt, and the mile roads.

A driver turning left across oncoming traffic, misjudging the speed of a motorcycle or not seeing it at all, is the recurring account in rider cases. Under Michigan law a driver must yield to oncoming traffic before turning left (MCL 257.650). Drivers turning into the retail strips on Grand River and Orchard Lake, and into the office campuses on Twelve Mile and Halsted at shift times, produce the same crash at lower speeds.
The freeways and the interchange.

On I-696, I-96, I-275, and M-5, drivers merging and changing lanes at the interchange at the city’s southwest corner, and rear-end crashes in stop-and-go traffic on I-696, are the rider’s risks; a rear-end impact a car absorbs throws a rider. Tractor-trailers heading to the Novi and Wixom corridor add blind spots and wind blast. See our
Farmington Hills truck accident page
The road itself.

A single-vehicle crash caused by a pothole, a broken concrete joint, a pavement drop-off, or a ridge left by road work is a claim against the agency with jurisdiction under the highway exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1402). In Farmington Hills that means three possible defendants:
MDOT

items.v: for I-696, I-96, I-275, M-5, and Grand River: written notice filed with the Court of Claims within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: The Road Commission for Oakland County

items.v: for Orchard Lake, Middlebelt, Inkster, Farmington Road, Halsted, Haggerty, and the mile roads, including Eight Mile and the 14 Mile roundabout: written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: The City of Farmington Hills

items.v: for subdivision and local streets: written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: A defect that was readily apparent to an ordinary observer for 30 days or more is conclusively presumed known to the agency (MCL 691.1403). Notice to the wrong agency is not notice.
Bars and restaurants.

31 percent of Michigan’s 2024 rider deaths involved alcohol. A bar or restaurant on Grand River or Orchard Lake that over-served the driver who hit a rider can be liable under the dram shop act: written notice within 120 days after you hire a lawyer, and suit within two years (MCL 436.1801(3)). sections.heading: Who pays a Farmington Hills rider’s medical bills

c.v: If a car or truck was involved, you have no-fault benefits, but not from your motorcycle insurer.
Under MCL 500.3114(5), your Personal Injury Protection benefits come, in order, from:

items.v: the insurer of the owner or registrant of the motor vehicle involved;
the insurer of that vehicle’s operator;
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s operator;
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s owner or registrant.

c.v: “Involved” does not require contact; a car that cut you off in the roundabout is involved even if it never touched you. If no insurer in that chain exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan pays (MCL 500.3172), with its $250,000 medical cap, unless you owned the motorcycle and it was uninsured (MCL 500.3113(b)).

The benefits are the ones a driver would get under MCL 500.3107: medical expenses up to the PIP limit on the policy that pays, 85 percent of lost wages for up to three years up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each year, $20 a day in replacement services, attendant care, and mileage. Written notice is due within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). See our
no-fault insurance claim page

The first medical limit is set by a policy you did not choose. Since the 2019 reform, the PIP medical level on the policy first in priority pays first; if the driver who hit you chose $250,000, that policy pays up to $250,000, and a lower-priority policy with more coverage, such as your own car policy, may then pay the rest.
If no car or truck was involved, no-fault does not apply.

A single-vehicle crash on a pothole, a broken joint, or gravel in the roundabout produces no PIP claim. Your bills go to your health insurance and any medical coverage you bought on the motorcycle policy, and your injury claim is against whoever caused the hazard. A rider hit by a car, by contrast, usually has a full PIP claim.
Your motorcycle.
Your own collision or comprehensive coverage pays for the bike. The mini tort claim does not cover a motorcycle, because a motorcycle is not a “motor vehicle” under the no-fault act (
Nerat v Swacker

sections.heading: Your claim against the driver who hit you

c.v: For pain and suffering and economic losses beyond no-fault, you sue the at-fault driver if your injury is a serious impairment of body function, permanent serious disfigurement, or death (MCL 500.3135(1)). Motorcycle injuries clear that threshold more often than car injuries: fractures, road rash requiring grafts, torn ligaments,
brain injuries
, and
spinal cord injuries

. You also recover excess economic damages above the PIP limit that applied to you, and wage loss above the no-fault cap or beyond three years (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)). You have three years to sue (MCL 600.5805(2)); a fatal crash is brought by the estate (see our
Farmington Hills wrongful death page
What the claim is worth depends on the other driver’s policy.
Many drivers carry the $50,000 opt-down minimum (MCL 500.3009(5)). The recovery then turns on your own
uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage
, which must be on the motorcycle policy; many car policies exclude the insured while riding an owned motorcycle. See our
uninsured motorist page
Comparative fault is the fight.

Above 50 percent at fault you recover no noneconomic damages; below that your award is reduced by your share, and at exactly 50 percent you recover half (MCL 500.3135(2)(b), 600.2959). Economic damages beyond no-fault are reduced by your share as well. Insurers argue speed, lane position, lane splitting (illegal in Michigan), and “came out of nowhere.” The police report, witnesses, the other driver’s phone records, business cameras along Orchard Lake and Grand River, and the rider’s own camera answer it.

Since 2012, Michigan has let riders 21 and older ride without a helmet if they carry at least $20,000 in first-party medical coverage and have either held a motorcycle endorsement for two years or passed an approved safety course (MCL 257.658). Riders under 21 must wear a helmet. If you met those conditions, riding helmetless was legal, so it was not a traffic violation. In a head-injury case the insurer will argue a helmet would have reduced the injury, which is a damages argument for the jury, not a bar; in a leg or shoulder case it is irrelevant.

faqs.question: A driver cut me off leaving the Orchard Lake roundabout. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Yes, if the driver exited or changed lanes across your lane. A motorcycle is entitled to the full lane, and the car is “involved” under no-fault whether or not it touched you, so its owner’s insurer is first in line for your medical bills. Get the plate and witnesses before the car is gone.

faqs.question: A car pulled out of a Michigan-left crossover and hit me. Who is at fault?

answer.v: Usually the driver leaving the crossover, who must yield to traffic in the lanes being entered. The police diagram, cameras at the nearby businesses, and witnesses decide it.

A motorcycle is not a “motor vehicle” under the no-fault act, so a rider who crashes alone has no PIP claim. A rider hit by a car or truck does: from that vehicle’s insurer first, under the priority rule.

faqs.question: I wasn’t wearing a helmet. Can I still recover?

answer.v: Yes, if you were 21 or older with the required $20,000 medical coverage and either two years of endorsement or a safety course. The insurer can argue a helmet would have reduced a head injury, which goes to damages, not to whether you have a claim.

faqs.question: I went down on a pothole on Middlebelt. Who do I notify?

answer.v: Middlebelt is generally a Road Commission for Oakland County road: written notice within 120 days stating the exact location, the defect, the injury, and the witnesses.

One year to notify the responsible no-fault insurer, three years to sue the at-fault driver, two years to sue a bar, 120 days for a notice to the City or the Road Commission, and 120 days to file notice of a road-defect claim against the State.
